However, there are rther research and regulation are required. tem · Film-former · Quality by Design (QbD) Terminology ODF is defined as “A thin layer or coating which is susceptible to being dissolved when in contact with a liquid” (Morath et al. In the United States Pharmacopeia, films are classified by their application site.

Accordingly, “oral film” is formulated to deliver medication into the mouth, such as oral hygiene products or medication to be delivered to the gastrointestinal tract for absorption. “Buccal film” and “sublingual films” are formulated to facilitate absorption through the proximal mucosal membranes avoiding firstpass metabolism or degradation in the gastrointestinal tract and providing a quick onset of action (USP 20.
The ODF is also referred to as “oral thin film”, “orally disintegrating film”, “oral dissolving film”, and “oral drug strip”.
The term “film” includes strips, sheets, and wafers, in any size and shape, including rectangular, square, or other desired shapes.
The films described herein can be any desired thickness and size that can be placed into the oral cavity of the user, with a thickness of from 20 to 300 microns.
Vol.:(01234567 3 52 Convenience ODF is a formulation that offers convenience of administration.

Oral dosage forms have been developed to provide easy drug administration to patients (Alopaeus et al. 2020; Vasvari et al. Around 60% of small molecule drugs currently on the market are administered via the oral route.

According to recent estimates, oral formulations account for 90% of the global market share of all pharmaceutical formulations intended for human use. Around 84% of the best-selling pharmaceutical products are oral dosage formulations, with a current value of US$35 billion and a 10% annual growth rate (Prasad et al. However, solid dosage forms such as capsules and tablets, which are the typical oral dosage form, can be difficult for young children and the elderly to take, especially those who have difficulty swallowing due to unconsciousness and dysphagia (Yir-Erong et al. Liquid formulation, oral disintegrating tablets (ODTs), and chewable tablets have been developed to address these challenges, but each has its limitations.
A better formulation for this problem is the ODF. ODFs provide more stable active ingredients than liquid dosage formulation and allow for more accurate dosing of an active ingredient.
ODFs have a less persistent oral sensation than ODTs and chewable tablets, are easier to store, and are less prone to breakage during distribution (Dixit and Puthli 20.
Compliance ODFs are ideal for pharmaceutical formulations because they can be produced and controlled under precise procedures and regulations.
For approval, ODF drugs must be produced, and quality controlled in the same certified good manufacturing practice facility as a regular drug, and the product must meet specified quality standards.
The European Pharmacopoeia defines ODFs as “Oromucosal preparations” with manufacturing, quality control, and labeling requirements (EP 10..

Quality control is an essential step in ensuring the safety and efficacy of pharmaceutical products (Patel et al. 20 and requires that the product is produced in a regulated and certified facility and is subject to regulatory quality control from production to market.

ODF products on the market ODFs have replaced many traditional oral solid dosage formulations due to their convenient administration and portability, as well as their advantageous drug absorption properties via buccal and sublingual routes.

Many ODFs have been approved as pharmaceuticals, starting with Pfizer’s Journal of Pharmaceutical Investigation (20 55:351–373 mouthwash Listerine PocketFax® Oral Care Strips, which were available over the counter (OTC) in 2004, through to the recently launched Ondansetron Rapid Film, which is an ethical drug (ETC) (Wasilewska and Winicka 20.

Table 1 summarizes the ODF products on the market, categorized as OTC and ETC. Oral route products Oral route ODFs use the same absorption mechanism as traditional oral medicines but have the advantage of rapidly disintegrating, dissolving, or dispersing in the mouth without the need for water, thereby delivering the active pharmaceutical ingredient (API) to the gastrointestinal tract in various forms (Chaturvedi et al. 2011; Borges et al. 2015; Speer et al. ODFs generally employ water-soluble polymers that cause the dosage form to be quickly hydrated by saliva and disintegrate within a few seconds, releasing the API on the tongue or in the oral cavity.

These advantages have led to the development of medicines for patients who need fast-acting medications or have difficulty swallowing or chewing, such as Zuplenz® for anti-nausea, Simpazan® for seizures and epilepsy, Nexedé® for non-steroidal antiinflammatory drugs, and Exervan® for amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (Dadey 2015; Soroushnai et al 2018; Wymer et al. Oral route ODFs are intended to produce absorption of APIs from the gastrointestinal tract rather than in the oral cavity (Sharma et al. Most ODFs developed for these medicinal products are licensed as generic versions of previously approved oral dosage drugs.
Therefore, it is desirable that the API is not eluted even if the formulation disintegrates in the oral cavity.
If it does, it is desirable that the API is not absorbed in the mouth, as the area under curve (AUC) and C of the pharmacokinetic values of the original drug must be bioequivalent.

It is therefore desirable that the API has a pKa value that is more readily eluted in the gastrointestinal tract than in the oral cavity, and that it does not aggregate in the oral cavity or adhere to mucous membranes.

Accordingly, for example, tadalafil ODF, the erectile dysfunction drug, has been developed and marketed in a formulation that is biologically equivalent to tadalafil tablets (Park et al. Buccal or sublingual route products Other drug delivery routes for ODFs include the buccal or sublingual route.

ODFs administered via the buccal or sublingual route typically have a double-layer structure consisting of a highly adhesive layer containing the API and less adhesive layer with low solubility, allowing effective delivery of the API to the buccal or sublingual glandular epithelium (Mukherjee and Bharath 20.

Once delivered to the epithelium, the API is efficiently delivered to the bloodstream due to the properties of mucosal tissue and the epithelial capillaries (Rathbone et al. 1994; Smart 19.

The buccal and sublingual epithelium are relatively soft, nonkeratinized tissues with wide intercellular spaces, strong adhesiveness, wide distribution of intraepithelial capillaries, and fast blood flow (Vijayabhaskar et al. APIs are delivered from the oral cavity into the capillaries through passive diffusion (Bobade et al. 2013; Thakur et al. The API is often hydrophobic, while the intercellular space is hydrophilic, so the API penetrates the cell and reaches the capillaries (Barua et al.20.

The buccal and sublingual mucosa have a thin membrane, many capillaries, and rapid blood flow, so it has excellent drug permeability and immediate absorption, resulting in high bioavailability (Dixit and Puthli 20.

For hydrophilic APIs, a size of 75–100 Da is suitable for passing through the intercellular space, whereas for hydrophobic APIs, there is relatively no limitation on molecular weight, but the lower the molecular weight, the better, and APIs larger than 1500 Da are not delivered efficiently (Bos and Meinardi 20.

The sedative Igalmi® and narcotic painkiller Suboxone® have been developed by exploiting these advantages (Igalmi 2016; Suboxone 20.
Formulation An ODF is a thin film formulation, so it is difficult to load a large amount of API into an ODF product.

Typically, the limit of API is 100 mg/strip, which can be further reduced or increased depending on the physicochemical characteristics, compatibility with excipients, and drug delivery pathways of the API (Venkateswarlu et al. The APIs currently used in ODFs are summarized in Table 2.
Typically, ODFs have a single film thickness of 100 μm or less and a weight of 300 mg or less, of which the limit for the loading amount of the API is 5–30%.

In addition, oral route ODFs typically have a low monolayer weight, because they need to disintegrate within 60 s, and buccal or sublingual route ODFs are typically multilayer films, so they have a lower percentage of actual drug entrapment.

Furthermore, APIs that require significant amounts of excipients such as surfactants for 3 56 API Dosage/unit physicochemical properties of APIs used in ODFs Apomorphine 10,15, 20, 25, Benzocaine 10 mg Buprenorphine 75, 150, 300, 4 600, 750, 900 Clobazam 5, 10, 20 mg Clonazepam 1, 2 mg Dexmedetomidine 0.12, 0.18 mg Dextromethorphan 10, 20 mg Dextromethorphan 7.5, 15 mg Diazepam 5, 10 mg Diphenhydramine 12.5, 19. 25 m Docusate 100 mg Donepezil 5, 10 mg Fentanyl 200, 400, 600, 800, 1200 μg Menthol 5, 25 mg Naloxone 0.7, 1 mg Ondansetron 4, 8 mg Phenylephrine 2.5, 10 mg Pyridoxine 100 mg Risperidone 1, 2 mg Sennosides 25 mg Sildenafil 25, 50, 100 mg Simethicone 62.5 mg Tadalafil 10, 20 mg *Experimental propety, **Predicted product stability can be difficult to incorporate into ODF formulations.

For this reason, it is difficult to load more than a limited amount of API into a single film, and it is not convenient for patients to take more than one strip, so 100 mg/ strip is usually the limit.
In addition, the dosage formulation must deliver the API, which must disintegrate or dissolve in the mouth and be saliva-soluble.

Because of the high oral exposure of the API compared with other dosage formulation, it is desirable that the API is non-irritating to the oral mucosa, or at least that the taste can be masked using excipients (Thakur et al. 2013; Nagendrakumar et al. Because of the direct exposure to the oral cavity, APIs that adhere to mucous membranes and cause a burning sensation or have an intolerable level of bitterness may have limited application.
In addition, for the drug to be absorbed by the designed route, the API must be readily soluble in saliva, stable in saliva, and have an appropriate molecular weight.
For example, if designed for the buccal or sublingual route, the molecular weight of the API should preferably be low enough to permeate mucous membranes.
If designed for the oral route, the molecular weight should preferably be high, as unexpected buccal absorption may occur.

Most of the main ingredients of ODFapproved drugs are poorly soluble in water, with a solubility of 3 g/L or less (Irfan et al. In the solvent casting method, which is the main film manufacturing method, API and excipients are dissolved or dispersed in water or a water/ethanol co-solvent system to prepare a casting solution (Morales and McConville 20.

During the mixing process of the casting solution, the API undergoes solubilization or partial solubilization under the influence of the solvent and excipients, which results in the unique physical properties of the film depending on the API solubility and ionization characteristics (Madhavi et al 2013; Garsuch and Breitkreutz 20.
Therefore, the water solubility and hydrophilic/hydrophobic property of the API are important factors in creating a homogeneous casting solution and product.

Since most APIs in the licensed products are poorly soluble and hydrophobic, a method for homogeneous dispersion is required (Karki et al. 2016; Godbole et al. 2018; Patil et al. For this process, surfactants or dispersion stabilizers may be required to homogeneously dissolve or disperse excipients, including the API, in the solvent, which may affect ODF weight and API load limits.
Therefore, when selecting an API, it is important to check its stability in water and its stability to heat, as the manufacturing process involves drying at high temperatures.

Based on solubility and permeability of a drug, the biopharmaceutics classification system (BCS) defines its physical properties, and most of the drugs used in ODFs belong to BCS class II or IV. To improve the solubility of these BCS class II or IV drugs, it is effective to apply solid dispersion technology to the film manufacturing method (Vasconcelos et al. 2007; Sheikh et al. 2020; Krull et al. 2015; Sievens-Figueroa et al. Among the solid dispersion technologies, polymers, surfactants, and organic solvents used in the solvent casting method are sufficiently applicable because they are highly compatible with the APIs used in film manufacturing.

Specifically, when solid dispersion film formulations containing compatible component polymers, surfactants, and organic solvents are sufficiently stirred, the main crystalline component (API) will undergo homogeneous distribution in the polymer matrix, which is further facilitated by the surfactants and plasticizers to produce the dispersion.
Once the solvent evaporates and the dispersion dries, it becomes amorphous (Brough and Williams 20.

If the raw materials for film formulation are made in a separate container and sufficiently dispersed, and the two solutions are mixed to produce a film by the solvent casting method, a more homogeneous ODF is produced with improved solubility and dissolution (Krull et al. 2016; Susarla et al. API limitations can be overcome by applying formulation technologies such as solid-lipid nanoparticles, lipid nanoparticles, liposomes, and hydrogels, including the solid dispersant technologies described above.

In particular, the incorporation of nanoparticle technology in the production of the APIs can result in improved drug solubility and permeability, controlled release, targeted delivery, taste masking, and long-term stability (Jacob et al. 2022; Nair et al. 2019; Kotta et al. Excipient ODFs must disintegrate or dissolve quickly under the conditions in the oral cavity, while still being film-like in their physical properties.

In particular, the product must be soft enough not to injure the oral cavity, but hard enough not to be brittle (Jacob et al. 2021; Liu et al. 2014; Semalty et al. Therefore, most ODFs are made from amorphous thermo-sensitive polymers.
Crystalline polymers are polymers with an ordered molecular structure that are relatively hard with a high melting point (Tm).

In contrast, amorphous polymers have an unordered molecular structure, and their Tm is difficult to define (Wang et al. 2006; Yang et al. 2010; Su et al. These polymers exist in a brittle glassy state at low temperatures, a soft rubbery state at temperatures above the glass transition temperature (Tg), and a viscous liquid state that liquefies at higher temperatures.

Therefor the temperature at which they liquefy is sometimes classified as their Tm (Albert et al. 2011a; Berry et al. 2007; Albert et al. 2011b; Seppala et al. 2012; Van den Mooter et al. 2001; Ambike et al. 2005; Aharoni 1985; Aharoni 19.

The reason for using thermoplastic polymers as film formers is to take advantage of their thermoplastic properties in the glassy transition state (Richard 1994; Keddie et al. 1994; Forrest et al. Unlike pure materials, which accumulate a certain amount of thermal energy during a state change, polymers are in a rubber-like state before the state change (Mahadevaiah et al. 2017; Dixit and Puthli 20.
In the glassy phase, the polymer is flexible, elastic, and fluid, while maintaining its shape and allowing migration between internal materials.
In this state, thermosets have fluidity in their cross-linked structure due to physical bonding, and thermoplastics have fluidity due to intermolecular entanglement.
These properties make thermosets easier to mold and make them suitable for mixing with API and other excipients (Jadhav et al. A variety of polymers are used in ODF formulations.
Pullulan is the most often used polymer as a film former.

It is a water-soluble polysaccharide produced by fermenting starch and forms a unique trio-structure by combining α-1,4 and 1,6 glycosidic, which has a high free volume (Bharathi et al. 2015; Nagar et al. 2011a, b; Leduy et al. In addition, it dissolves well at high and low temperatures, has little taste or aroma, and has relatively high thermal stability, so it is very useful (Singh et al. Furthermore, since pullulan does not have branching, physical control and analogy using additives are easy, and oxygen permeability is markedly reduced, so that the stability of the API is greatly increased.
As an oxygen barrier, it is 300 times stronger than hydroxypropyl methylcelluloses (HPMC) film and 9 times stronger than gelatin film (Saini 20.
Even if pullulan is used alone as a film former, the film product exhibits excellent mechanical properties and has good compatibility with various APIs.

It is widely used as a health food excipient because it dissolves faster than other film formers such as HPMC and leaves less residue (Singh et al. Pectin is water-soluble, contains an ester group and a carboxyl group, and is divided into high and low methoxy pectin.
It is sometimes used as an amide vector containing an amide group (Pathare et al. High methoxy pectic is esterified by 50% and low methoxy pectin is esterified by less than 50%.

Pectin interacts with divalent or higher cations via negative charges within carboxyl groups in aqueous solutions to form gelatinized or eggbox structures, 3 58 and the drug release profile can also be adjusted by using this property (Cao et al. In general, pectin has good film-forming ability and produces a high level of hardness, even when manufactured thinly (Van Rooyen et al. In addition, it has the cost advantage of being able to use it by subdividing specifications.
However, it is sensitive to pH, which can affect drug elution characteristics, and has the disadvantage of being somewhat astringent and bitter, and difficult to process due to its hardness.

It can also be used together with other film substrates to improve the physical properties of the film (Legrand 1969; Ghaffari et al. Gum polysaccharides can be used as a film-forming agent or viscosity regulator to improve the mechanical properties and texture of the ODF and to improve mucosal adhesion properties (Alaei et al. 2021; Prezotti et al. Mucosal adhesion can maintain contact with tissue and induce controlled drug release with the ability of the film to stick to the mucosal surface in the mouth (Xu et al. Examples of gum polysaccharides commonly used in ODFs include xanthan gum, carrageenan, and gelan gum (Achayuthakan and Suphantharika 2008; Lafargue et al. When an ODF is formulated, gum polysaccharides have different physical properties depending on their type.

However, due to many branches, the structure is complicated, the free volume is large, and the Tg is low. Although Tg varies slightly depending on molecular weight, the Tg of Carrageenan is ~ 80 °C, while the Tg of HPMC is 170–198 °C (Zhang et al. High viscosity is produced by complex structures and intermolecular attraction when a gum polysaccharide is dispersed or dissolved, and the dried composition is close to a gel. Therefore, it is added in a smaller amount than a single polymer ODF and is used to reduce cracking due to low free volume or to provide softness.
It is also used as a binder when using a polymer with a large molecular weight or a main component that is not compatible with a solvent, by utilizing viscosity generated by the complex structure.
Depending on the positioning of polymers and additives, the free volume is rather low, which can increase hardness and reduce the rate of collapse or dissolution.

Unlike other natural polymers, chitosan is protonated in acidic conditions and becomes positively charged (Ibrahim et al. Since the epithelium is negatively charged, chitosan ODFs are highly adhesive (Luo et al. It also produces excellent binding to partially negatively charged APIs or additives, which can be used to control drug elution or increase oral absorption efficiency (Qin et al. However, chitosan is water-insoluble in alkaline conditions.
Even if it is soluble in acidic conditions, it has a major disadvantage of being too astringent, so there are many factors to consider when using it as film former (Chun and Choi 20.
HPMCs are colorless, odorless, water-soluble polymers that are classified according to alkyl groups and viscosity Journal of Pharmaceutical Investigation (20 55:351–373 grades (Felton 20.

They have a relatively high Tg, low adhesion and strength, but are flexible and have a high carrying capacity, making them suitable for controlling the release profile of APIs (Cilurzo et al. HPMC forms its own gel network by hydrogen bonding within hydroxyl groups, and hydrophobic interaction and hydrophobic substitution are also suitable for dispersion stabilization of hydrophilic and hydrophobic substances (Joshi 20.
These properties increase the versatility of API and excipient selection, affect the carrying capacity and elution retardation of API, and improve the dispersion stability (Jadach et al 20.

HPMCs used in ODFs are typically low viscosity grades due to the convenience of the manufacturing process, including water dispersion and drying, but high viscosity grades are often used in blends, to control drug release.

Hydroxypropylcelluloses (HPCs) are cellulose derivatives that are both water-soluble and fat-soluble, and are commonly categorized as L, M, or H depending on the degree of substitution (Cilu et al. Low-substituted HPCs are less water-soluble because of the crystalline nature of cellulose, and depending on their grade, there are differences in the binding force such as hydrogen bonding between the HPCs or between additives, so L-HPC has a significantly higher Tg of ~ 220 °C. In contrast the Tg of M/L-HPC is relatively low at ~ 105 °C (Kaur et al. Due to their binding capacity, HPCs gel easily and usually form a colloidal solution in water below 38 °C, but precipitate in a swollen form at about 40–45 °C (Eshtiaghi et al. 2010; Kawano et al. Depending on the drug, HPCs are usually added as a material to increase hardness.
HPCs are also suitable as a single film former, but the choice of plasticizer type and total amount must be carefully considered.

Methylcellulose (MC) is a cellulose derivative containing a methoxide group, which has slightly higher water solubility compared with HPCs, and precipitates in a swollen form above a certain temperature but has a slightly higher critical point of ~ 55 °C (Dürig and Karan 20.
Compared with HPMC, MC has a lower gelation threshold and poorer solubility in cold water.

In addition, compared with HPMC, MC has a large viscosity change with temperature, low adhesion, enzyme resistance, and water-retaining property (Ergun et al. Due to these properties, it is more commonly used as a dispersion stabilizer, binder, and elution control additive than as a film formation.

Starch has different physical properties including crystal structures depending on the raw material, but generally has very low flexibility and hardness (Krogars et al. The development of ODFs using various starches, such as cassava, sweet potato, and corn, has been reported (Sha et al. 2022; Bensaad et al. 2022; Queiroz et al. Among them, cassava starch ODFs have superior physical properties to other starch ODFs and are economical, especially when Lycoat, a hydroxypropyl starch, is used in film formation.
Consequently, it is typically used alone as a binder, disintegrant, and viscosity improver, or in combination with pectin to increase the hardness of the film.

The cross-linked sodium carboxymethylcellulose is used as a super disintegrating agent and its fast disintegration derives from its quick swelling, porosity, and capillary action (Jadhav et al. It is generally used to increase the disintegration rate of fast-disintegrating ODFs.

Due to the electrochemical properties of the carboxymethyl group, carboxymethylcellulose (CMC) can increase dispersion stability and can be gelated and aggregated using metal ions and linkers (Arumughan et al. CMC is considered a fast-disintegrating ODF due to its relatively high solubility, but as it has the same charge as the epithelium, it may have low mucosal adhesion (Podczeck et al. Depending on the characteristics of the API, CMC can be used for delivery by itself, and with polymers and linkers of opposite charge to control elution, but there are other factors to consider, such as the dissociation conditions of the complex.
The film-forming polymers used in ODFs have a common characteristic of hygroscopic expansion and disintegration.
Therefore, ODFs are hygroscopic, which makes them highly environmentally sensitive and difficult to store for long periods.

To solve this problem, ODFs are usually packed individually, which increases the cost of the product and requires separate physical properties of the ODF for mass production compatibility on the packing machine, which, in some cases, may decrease the quality of the product.

Plasticizers used in films change the Tg of the film former (Kang et al. Plasticizers make hydrogen bonds between the API and the hydroxyl groups of polymers, increasing the atomic interactions but reducing the atomic energy and homogeneously accommodating the API and plasticizer inside the polymer bulky spaces (Fong et al. This space provides flexibility and elasticity and lowers the Tg. Edible plasticizers include sugar alcohols, whereby the smaller the molecular weight, the better the opportunity for contact with the polymeric hydroxy groups, which reliably imparts plasticity (Johns et al. However, when two or more polymers are included, polymers with relatively weak plasticizing effect-polymer attraction are separated, so it is necessary to control the number of other excipients (Sun et al. If an excessive amount of plasticizer is added, a plasticizer-plasticizer interaction is formed, which is visible on dried film products. and there are unwanted properties like high flexibility and stickiness (Mascia et al. For this reason, plasticizers are used in initial film development in amounts of 10% by weight of the film former, and small amounts of sugar alcohols are usually used in combination with glycerin and D-sorbitol, which is more effective (Cherian et al. Solid sugar alcohols such as mannitol and xylitol are also commonly used for texture, sweetening, and plasticizing effects.
A combination of solid and liquid plasticizer facilitates better film formation with reduced flexibility and stickiness.
Other types of excipients used in ODF formulation include solubilizers, because many APIs are hydrophobic, and surfactants to reduce the surface tension of the casting solution.

The type and amount used are determined based on the physicochemical properties of the API. Due to the nature of ODF formulations, flavors and sweeteners are used to mask the irritating properties inherent in hydrophobic materials as they are tasted during ingestion.

Common sweeteners include acesulfame-K, sucralose, aspartame, and stevia, although a combination is sometimes used because different ingredients have different sweetness intensities and taste perception rates (Gwak et al. One material that can be used for multiple purposes is cyclodextrin.
Cyclodextrin has a donut-like structure with a hydrophobic interior and a hydrophilic exterior.

Therefore, the main hydrophobic component binds to the hydrophobic donut through hydrophobic interactions, forming a conjugate (Park et al. It has a good masking effect to help solubilize the main ingredient and reduce the bitterness and burning sensation of the main ingredient.

Cyclodextrin is categorized into α-(6), β-(7), and γ-(8) depending on the number of glucoses unit, the basic constituent monomer, and the higher the number of monomers, the larger the cavity diameter.

In general, the β-type is used for certain ingredients in medicines or foods, and different types are used depending on the molecular weight of the main ingredient (Liu et al. The excipients used in other drug formulation often serve different purposes in ODFs.
The excipients used in approved ODF medicines are categorized according to purpose of use (see Tables 3 and 4).
The type and dosage of excipients appropriate for the target product are determined by thorough research.

The moisture content of ODFs is a very important parameter.
The moisture content has a significant impact on the mechanical strength, adhesion, and brittleness of the film (Gorle and Gattani 20.
ODFs contain between 5 and 14% moisture, depending on the product.
If the moisture content is low, the film will be brittle.
If the moisture content is high, its stickiness will cause problems during packaging and during product consumption.
In the product manufacturing process, the moisture content determines the process-time of the drying and affects the shelf life of the product.

In general, the moisture content of an ODF is determined by methods such as Karl Fischer titration or thermogravimetric analysis (Visser et al. Thermogravimetric analysis is performed by the drying reduction test method, which measures the amount of moisture in the sample that is lost when it is dried under the prescribed conditions (MFDS 20.
A relatively simple method, the paper moisture meter, can also be used for quick measurements.
To evaluate the mechanical properties, the 3 62 tensile strength, elongation at break, yield stress, Young’s modulus, and folding endurance can be measured (Morales and McConville 20.
Except for folding endurance, these methods require measurement equipment and are of limited practical use as evaluation criteria in ODF development.
The folding endurance is measured by repeatedly folding the film at a 180° angle at the same point until it breaks, without any measuring equipment (Dixit and Puthli 2009; Garsuch and Breitkreutz 20.
From the measurement results, the strength and flexibility of the film can be evaluated to determine whether the product can be produced consistently.
It is not practical to evaluate all the properties listed above during product production.
Some of the above parameters are considered in the ODF design and development stages.

The weight, thickness, moisture content, folding endurance, and so on, are used as evaluation parameters during the production process as it is relatively easy and quick to evaluate the ODF. To examine the chemical properties ODFs, including the surface and internal structure and compatibility of an ODF, scanning electron microscope (SEM), X-ray diffraction (XRD), Fourier transform-infrared spectroscopy (FT-IR), and differential scanning calorimetry (DSC), etc., are used (Chandra et al. SEM analysis can determine the surface morphology, particle size, distribution, internal structure, and bonding state of the film, as well as the homogeneity of the active ingredients in the film.

It examines surface contamination, obtains information about microstructures and reveals spatial variations in chemical substances (Khan et al. 2015; Hoang et al. XRD analysis can confirm the crystallinity or amorphousness of the main components in the film.
DSC analysis reveals the thermal stability and thermal changes in the film and, like XRD, the degree of amorphization of the active ingredient.

FT-IR is performed to determine the suitability, bonding, or interaction of drugs and excipients in the final formulation, which is evaluated by grinding a small sample of the product and performing a spectral scan using KBr pellets.
Chemical characterization is often performed for research purposes and is not appropriate for drug development for licensing purposes.
The assay, content uniformity, disintegration, dissolution, and stability tests are essential evaluations for developing ODFs for licensing purposes.
Assay is an important evaluation indicator of drug efficacy.
It is evaluated by referring to the standardized analytical methods of the main ingredients listed in each country’s pharmacopoeia.

It is measured using high pressure liquid chromatography (HPLC) or ultraviolet (UV) spectrometer equipment by adopting a pretreatment method that effectively extracts the drug from the formulation (Mohamed et al. Content uniformity is also a critical ODF parameter because it can be used to estimate the accuracy of dosing.

Due to the nature of Journal of Pharmaceutical Investigation (20 55:351–373 ODFs, uniformity is not determined by measuring the mass of the ODF and calculating the mass deviation, but rather by conducting the assay to determine content uniformity.

At least 30 samples are taken, and for 10 of them, the assay of the main ingredient in each formulation is measured by an appropriate method, and the degree of uniformity is evaluated by calculating the acceptability constant.
Disintegration and dissolution are experimental items that can predict the behavior of a drug in vivo.

Experiments are performed to determine the release rate and in vivo profile of a drug (Kanna et al. Disintegration is the process by which a solid dosage form breaks down into smaller particles in gastric or intestinal fluids, thereby increasing the particle surface area required for drug dissolution.
Pharmacopoeia disintegration apparatus can also be used to study the disintegration time.

It is defined as the time it takes for the ODF to completely disintegrate without leaving a solid residue, as observed on visual inspection under temperature conditions of 37.0 ± 0.5 °C using a disintegration tester with water or artificial saliva.
The ideal disintegration time for fast dissolving oral thin films is between 5 and 30 s, although disintegration within 60 s is acceptable (Jaiswal 20.

Disintegration can be measured relatively easily by the petri dish method, in which 2 ml of distilled water are added to a petri dish and the ODF is placed on the surface of the water, with the time to disintegration measured; and by the drop method, in which a drop of distilled water is pipetted onto the ODF placed in a flat petri dish, and the time to the formation of a hole in the ODF is measured.

This can be used to compare the disintegration of different formulation ratios during the development phase (Maheswari et al. 2014; Kianfar et al. Dissolution is the process by which a solute dissolves in a solvent to become a solution.

Dissolution experiments for ODFs are typically performed following pharmacopeia requirements for solid oral dosage forms using a basket or paddle apparatus in an environment adjusted to 37 °C (pH 6.8 phosphate buffer or artificial saliva) (Speer et al 2019a, b).

Individual films are placed in the dissolution test solution and a suitably timed aliquot is withdrawn periodically, and the dissolution medium is replenished accordingly (Dixit and Ruthli 2009; Kumria et al. 2013; Mazumder et al. The obtained solutions are analyzed using validated analytical methods of HPLC or UV spectrophotometer at specific wavelengths.
Due to the nature of the formulation, the film may float in the medium, stick to the container, or fold in on itself during the experiment, making data reproducibility difficult.
In this case, rounding the film into a cylindrical shape and placing it in a sinker for experimentation can yield highly reproducible results.

The dissolution media, pH of the media and rotational speed are required to be developed and validated so that the developed ODF can produce a dissolution rate in the range of 70–85% within Journal of Pharmaceutical Investigation (20 55:351–373 one hour.

The stability of the product is evaluated by examining the color, weight, and API assay of the product after at least 12 months of storage at 25 ± 2 °C (60 ± 5% RH) and 6 months at 40 ± 2 °C (75 ± 5% RH).
No change in assessments over time indicates compliance (Sharma et al. Because ODFs are dissolved in the mouth, cytotoxicity, palatability, and other factors are evaluated.

For drug approval, oral solid dosage forms are required to submit topical toxicity test data if mucosal irritation is expected, so cytotoxicity tests are often performed using tongue epithelial cell lines to confirm the cytotoxic properties of the film.
It is also necessary to evaluate palatability, including taste.

Palatability evaluation can be done by selecting a group of people to fill out a questionnaire after taking the product, which includes indicators such as taste, aftertaste, mouthfeel, and ease of acceptance (Shet and Vaidya 20.
Although palatability is an important aspect of ODF evaluation, as with physical properties, it is difficult to provide general criteria.

There are methods such as electronic tongue devices and questionnaires, but they are difficult to set as evaluation items and are developed considering the characteristics of medicine taking (Kayumba 20.
Regulatory requirements for ODFs The methods presented above have practical difficulties for establishing quality standards for the actual product when it is released.

It is difficult to set a generalized standard because there is no standard applicable to all films, and the properties vary depending on the properties of the main component and the type and content of polymers and plasticizers compatible with the main component properties (Yir-Erong et al. Pharmacopoeias such as the European Pharmacopoeia, US Pharmacopeia and MFDS provide monographs for common dosage forms, but monographs and standards for oral thin films have not yet been established.

So, there are inadequacies in the pharmaceutical technical procedures for analysis and quality control of oral films (Mazumder et al. The European Pharmacopoeia states that oral films should have “adequate mechanical strength to withstand handling without being damaged.” There is no standard for what constitutes adequate mechanical strength and how dissolution testing should be performed (EP 20.

The Korean Pharmacopoeia states that ODFs should be suitable for testing according to the Uniformity of Preparations Test Act, unless otherwise specified, and that appropriate disintegration and dissolution tests are specified in each article, and that preparations should be preserved in airtight containers; but there are no standards for quality control methods.
Therefore, at present, ODFs tend to use the test methods recommended for oral solid dosage forms such as tablets and capsules (MFDS 20.

Currently, the quality evaluation test items for ODF finished pharmaceutical products include characterization, confirmation test, purity test to evaluate flexible substances, drying reduction, assay, disintegration or dissolution test, and uniformity test as evaluation items, and set standards and test methods.

ODF development with quality‑by‑design (QbD) QbD overview QbD is a pharmaceutical quality management system that aims to anticipate, systematically control, and respond to risks that may arise during the research phase and manufacturing process, with the ultimate goal of providing patients with safe and effective drugs.

By applying QbD, the goal is to improve and maintain drug quality, reduce patient risk from low-quality drugs, and ensure the continuous production of high-quality drugs (Jin et al. 2014; Lee et al. To develop a drug product using QbD, a quality target product profile (QTPP) must first be defined and validated, and critical quality attributes (CQAs) must be established based on prior knowledge and experience for the stated purpose.

By defining critical material attributes (CMAs) and factors affecting critical process parameters (CPPs) that can affect the CQA of a drug product, it is possible to find solutions to problems, manage risks, and produce homogeneous quality drug products (Lee et al. 2022; Guideline 20.
There are also economic benefits from the perspective of shortening development time by reducing the time required for scale-up and technology transfer (Kourti and Davis 20.
For these reasons, many countries require QbD-based drug development and management, and it has become an essential quality assurance standard in the global pharmaceutical market.
The application of QbD in ODF development is also necessary.

Application of QbD in ODF development Typically, QbD starts with establishing a clear QTPP, which is a summary of the predicted quality characteristics of a drug product that must be achieved to meet target quality standards of safety and efficacy.
A QTPP is analogous to the contents of the medicine manual enclosed when purchasing prescription drugs (Marto et al. 2015; Finkler and Krummen 20.
Usually, indication, dosage form, administration route, pharmacokinetics, appearance, and assay are included (Zurdo et al. 2015; Gupta and Jhawat 20.
To clearly define QTPP, it is necessary to consider the nature of the ODF, the development and manufacturing environment, and identify the QTPPs that are important from the patient’s perspective.
A comprehensive overview of the ideal characteristics that a drug product should achieve when developing 3 64 a drug with ODFs is provided in Table 5.
CQA must be within the definition of a QTPP to ensure that the physical, chemical, and pharmaceutical properties of the drug product meet the targeted product quality.

CQAs can be understood as target results in a drug product’s certificate of analysis, and CQAs contain an additional item asking whether it is a CQA, with the corresponding justification written according to the target standard (Lee et al. Potential CQAs of the finished product can be derived from previous scientific information and experience, but the potential CQAs should be selected according to the QTPP (Mandenius 2009; Rathore 20.
Table 6 summarizes the items that should be considered CQAs for ODFs.
Appearance, identification, loss on drying, analysis, degradation, and so on, can be considered CQAs to reach the target QTPP.

In the CQA selection phase, the CQA is selected by determining and justifying the risk for each quality characteristic item based on the results of analytical and statistical processing of the influence of raw material, formulation, and process variables to achieve the target quality defined by the QTPP (Pramod et al. For a specific example, in ODF, assay and content uniformity are important quality assessment that affect safety and efficacy, so they can be selected as CQAs.

However, since the identification test only needs to confirm the presence or absence of active ingredients, it does not have a significant impact on formulation and process variables, so it is only selected as a quality attribute, not a CQA. By performing risk assessment (RA), the CMAs and CPPs that affect CQAs can be identified.

Among the independent variables that affect the CQA of a finished drug product, variables such as the physicochemical properties of the API and excipients are CMAs, while manufacturing process parameters are CPPs.
Identifying CMAs and CPPs in the early stages of development helps set the development direction and design space appropriately (Kelley et al. 2016; Raina et al. 2017; Braem and Turner 2019; Chen 20.

To select CMAs and CPPs, a high-level understanding of the process should be sought through a combination of design of experiment (DoE), statistical modelling, mathematical modelling, and studies that evaluate the underlying mechanisms (Lee et al. To identify and evaluate CMAs and CPPs that affect CQA, an Ishikawa fishbone or process map about material attributes (MAs) and process parameters (PPs) are used to identify risks.
It lists all the potential variables in the formulation and manufacturing process that can affect drug product quality.

Figure 1 maps the anticipated risks of developing ODFs by the casting solvent method, a typical production method for ODF, using the Ishikawa fishbone (Borges et al. In Table 7, the MA and PP factors that could potentially affect CQAs are risk analyzed using the preliminary hazard analysis (PHA) tool, and categorized as high, medium, or low risk.

As the application of QbD is intended to proactively detect and manage factors with Journal of Pharmaceutical Investigation (20 55:351–373 potential risk (high and medium), an initial screening study is conducted to ensure that the selected factors affect the CQA of the product within a set range (Lee et al. PHA can be useful for analyzing existing systems or for prioritizing risks in situations where more extensive techniques are not available.

Tools such as failure mode effects analysis (FMEA) can then be used to take actions such as DoE. FMEA allows the prioritization of risks and monitoring of the effectiveness of risk management activities.

Among the MAs containing APIs and excipients, FMEA is used to select the CMA. Similarly, FMEA is used to select CPPs that are part of a unit production process, and the FMEA RA determines whether the CPP requires a DoE. In this way, the CMAs and CPPs that require DoE for the major hazards are selected.

With each CMA and CPP finally selected by RA as independent variable x and CQA as dependent variable y, the design space is established by identifying the interrelationships related to CQA satisfying the QTPP in a multidimensional combination.
The design space, which represents a multidimensional combination, enables the manufacturing of products that are suitable for the set QTPP and CQA (Lee and Kim 20.
After the design space has been established, if the process is operated within these limits, PV is performed to demonstrate the provision of acceptable quality (Rathore 20.

This enables the control and operational space to be established, and the drug to be produced to satisfy QTPP and CQA with consistent quality within each of the established ranges (Lee et al.
